pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret it as magnitude in context; distinguish absolute-value comparisons from ordering statements.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): supports work on negatives and number-line reasoning; absolute value as magnitude underpins later work (bounds, error, modulus).
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.7c — 'understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation' and 7d distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
• Operational details: Define |x| as DISTANCE from zero (always ≥0), so |−5| = |5| = 5. Keep the distinction sharp between magnitude (how far) and order (which is greater): −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|. Ground in context — a debt of −£30 is a bigger amount than −£5 even though it is 'less'. Read |·| aloud as 'distance from zero'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'What is |−8|?' Tier B: 'Which is greater: −9 or −2? Which has the greater absolute value?' Tier C: 'A balance of −£40 vs −£15 — which is the larger debt, and which is the smaller number? Explain.'
bestPractices: Define absolute value strictly as distance from zero on the number line, so it is never negative and |−5| = |5|
Hold magnitude and order apart explicitly with paired statements (−7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|)
Anchor in contexts where magnitude matters (size of a debt, depth below sea level) versus signed order
Read |x| aloud as 'the distance of x from zero' rather than 'make it positive' (a rule that hides the meaning)
Use symmetric points about zero to show two different numbers share one absolute value
keyRepresentations: Number line with a distance arc from 0 to the point (length = |x|)
Mirror/fold about zero showing −a and a mapping to the same distance
Context strips (debt size, depth) where magnitude is the salient quantity
Paired statement cards contrasting order (<, >) with absolute value (|·|)
commonMisconceptions: Believing |x| just 'removes the minus sign' as a symbol trick rather than measuring distance (fails for expressions like |x−3|)
Thinking the number with the greater absolute value is automatically the greater number (−9 > −2)
Assuming absolute value can be negative

learn.summary: For learners aged 11–12: build absolute value as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0, so |−5| = |5| = 5), interpret it as magnitude in real contexts (size of a debt, depth below sea level), and keep it sharply separate from ordering (−7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|). Read |x| aloud as 'the distance of x from zero', not 'make it positive'. A manipulable number line is the core activity; an annotated static line, a consolidation set of short items, and a context dialogue are supporting approaches with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Measure distance from zero on a draggable number line
feedback: If the learner expects |x| to carry a minus sign on the left of zero, point to the arc: it is a length, so it reads the same magnitude on both sides.
When the arc for −9 is longer than for −2, ask them to say aloud which number is greater (−2) and which is further from zero (−9) — two different answers.
At the crossing point, highlight that |x| touches 0 exactly at zero, then grows again in either direction.
activities.rationale: Absolute value is defined as distance from zero on the number line; making that distance visible and live as the point moves ties the symbol to its meaning and separates magnitude from order. The dragging/mirror/dual-read-out details are illustrative affordances, not required technology, and are a research-informed proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
KS3 number work develops reasoning with negative numbers and magnitude on the number line, underpinning absolute value / modulus.
learnerActions: Drag a point along a number line and watch a glowing arc from 0 to the point report its length as |x|, which is positive on either side of zero and is 0 only when the point is at zero.
Park the point at −5, then flip on a mirror toggle so the reflection at +5 lays down an identical arc — observe |−5| = |5| = 5.

Read a twin read-out that shows the signed value beside its absolute value; move the point to −9 then to −2 and notice the arc for −9 is LONGER even though −9 sits further LEFT (is the smaller number).
Drag the point across zero and watch the |x| read-out shrink to 0 and climb again — distance tracks how far from zero, never which side.
activities.intendedInsight: Absolute value is a distance (a length) from zero: it is never negative, two symmetric points share one absolute value, and 'further from zero' is a different question from 'greater number'.

activities.title: Annotated number line with distance arcs (static anchor)
feedback: If a learner reads the longer arc as 'the bigger number', separate the two questions: length of arc = magnitude; position left/right = order.
Confirm both arcs for −5 and 5 are the same length before moving on.
activities.rationale: A static annotated line anchors the distance meaning and the two-numbers-one-magnitude idea; it supports the same objective as the draggable version without live dragging and works on paper. It lacks the live across-zero movement, so add tracing tasks if used alone.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: On a number line, mark −5 and 5 and draw the arc from 0 to each, confirming both measure 5 units.
Reveal a callout that contrasts the order statement (−5 < 5) with the magnitude statement (|−5| = |5|).
For a second pair such as −9 and −2, draw both arcs and state separately which number is greater (−2) and which has the greater absolute value (−9).
activities.intendedInsight: Even without live movement, measuring arcs from zero establishes 'distance from zero' and the idea that two different numbers can share one absolute value.

activities.title: Consolidation: evaluate and discriminate
feedback: If a learner answers the same way to '−9 > −2' and '|−9| > |−2|', reread each using the number line: position for order, distance from zero for absolute value.
If an absolute value is given as negative, restate |x| as a length that cannot be negative.
activities.rationale: Evaluation and magnitude-vs-order discrimination are cleanly checkable in short structured items, making this a useful consolidator after the distance meaning is established. Recognition and selected-response items chiefly check and reinforce classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent reasoning or construction, which the number-line work is intended to develop.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: Match signed values to their absolute values.
Judge paired true/false statements such as '−9 > −2' (false) versus '|−9| > |−2|' (true), and explain each by the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the distance meaning is built, learners can reliably compute absolute values and tell absolute-value comparisons apart from ordering comparisons.

activities.title: Context talk: larger debt vs larger number
feedback: If the learner equates 'bigger debt' with 'bigger number', place −40 and −15 on a line: −40 sits further left, so it is the smaller number though the larger debt.
Encourage the learner to state the two questions separately before answering.
activities.rationale: Grounding magnitude in debt/depth/temperature contexts targets the common conflation of magnitude with order and gives learners language for the distinction. Dialogue here addresses the contextual magnitude-vs-order question and works alongside the spatial number-line model; its advantage over other media is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: Discuss a scenario: 'You owe £40, I owe £15 — whose debt is bigger, and whose balance is the greater number?'
Explain that −40 is the larger debt (greater magnitude) yet the smaller/lower balance (−40 < −15).
Try a second context (−8°C vs −3°C, or a diver at −8 m vs −3 m): name who is deeper/colder/further from zero and whose value is the greater number.
activities.intendedInsight: In real contexts, magnitude (how far from zero) and order (which value is greater) answer different questions, and conflating them produces errors like '−40 is the greater number'.

constraints: Define |x| strictly as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0); avoid teaching it as 'remove the minus sign', which hides the meaning and fails for expressions like |x−3|.
Always pair order and magnitude explicitly (e.g. −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|) so learners do not assume greater absolute value means greater number.
Distinguish |−5| from −5: they are not interchangeable.
Recognition/matching/true-false items consolidate and check classification but do not elicit independent construction; use them after the number-line meaning is built, not as the primary teaching.
The static annotated line is a scaffold that lacks live movement across zero; if used alone, add tasks where learners trace the distance changing on both sides of zero.
A 3D representation was judged to add little because absolute value is a one-dimensional distance; this is a design judgement for this topic, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited standards sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat the citations as unconfirmed.
The original rated a quiz and a 3D interactive by catalog 'fit'; those ranking labels were removed and the quiz and dialogue retained as supporting approaches with distinct pedagogical purposes.
Arithmetic and logic checked: |−8| = 8; −3 > −8 while |−8| > |−3|; −40 < −15 while |−40| > |−15|; −5 < 5 with |−5| = |5| — all consistent across every action, feedback item and note.

probeDeeper: On a number line, which is further from zero, −8 or −3?
Can an absolute value ever be negative? Why not?
A diver at −8 m and one at −3 m: who is deeper, who is further from the surface, and whose depth is the 'bigger' number?
assess.correctAnswer: −3 is the greater number (it is closer to zero / further right on the number line). But −8 has the greater absolute value, because |−8| = 8 and |−3| = 3 — absolute value is distance from zero, ignoring direction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude: '−8 is greater than −3 because 8 > 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on a number line: −3 sits to the right of −8, so −3 is greater. Reason from position, not digit size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks −8 above −3 when asked which is the greater number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks absolute value keeps the sign: |−8| = −8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define absolute value as distance from zero — a length, never negative. Read |−8| off the number line as 8 units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a negative absolute value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes greater absolute value means greater number (treats the two comparisons as identical)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a context (−8°C vs −3°C): −8 is colder/lower yet 'further from zero'. Name the two different questions explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives the same answer to both questions.

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by magnitude or gives a negative absolute value; treats the two comparisons as the same.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes ordering (−3 > −8) from absolute value (|−8| > |−3|), defines |x| as distance from zero, and applies both correctly in context.
responseLevels.partial: Computes absolute values correctly but still conflates 'greater absolute value' with 'greater number' in context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Which is the greater number, −8 or −3? And which has the greater absolute value? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for BOTH the ordering and the absolute value in one prompt forces the child to separate 'which is bigger' from 'which is further from zero'. A child conflating them gives the same answer twice; a child who understands gives opposite answers and can justify each by the number line.
